item.title: The Psychology and Psychotherapy of Procrastination
item.description:
Procrastination

The Psychology and Psychotherapy of Procrastination

Comprehending the underlying dynamics of procrastination is key to treating it.

Posted August 22, 2026

Key points
  • Procrastination is an archetypal pattern of human behavior.
  • Accepting life's routine tedium can help in conquering procrastination.
  • Overcoming procrastination requires conscious, mindful presence.

This is Part 2 of a series about procrastination.

"Sisyphus" by Titian
Source: Wikimedia Commons/Public Domain

In Part 1 of this series, we discussed the phenomenon of procrastination, its causes and vicissitudes. Procrastination is one of the most ubiquitous complaints psychotherapists hear from clients or patients. What is the underlying psychology of procrastination? And how can it be conquered?

Dealing With the Unconscious "Inner Child"

Commonly, procrastination stems from an unconscious conflict between our mature and responsible "adult self," who knows what needs to be done, and our irresponsible and impulsive "inner child." (See my prior post.) As with real children, without adequate adult supervision and guidance, the "inner child" will naturally resist tedium or routine, preferring fun, entertaining, pleasurable, stimulating activities instead.

This is natural and in keeping with Freud's (1911) concept of the pleasure principle: We instinctively avoid pain and seek pleasure. If an activity or task is not fun, fascinating, engaging, or pleasurable, why do it? Children must be disciplined, motivated, or coerced to do tedious chores like cleaning their rooms, brushing their teeth, doing their homework, etc. This is a fundamental part of parenting. It is the same for grown-ups, since if there is not a well-developed and conscious adult part of the personality to oversee, supervise, and lovingly discipline the impetuous inner child, difficult, tedious or boring chores will be avoided as long as humanly possible, because it is the unconscious so-called "inner child," rather than the adult self, who is running the show or calling the shots.

In therapy, the patient must become more conscious of these disparate parts of themselves, these complexes, and the more mature, adult part of the personality must take charge of properly parenting and disciplining the inner child and making mindful, responsible adult decisions that minimize or preclude daily procrastination.

Accepting and Embracing Existential Tedium

Another existential conceptualization of procrastination is what I call the Sisyphus syndrome. As punishment by the gods, Sisyphus was fated to eternally roll a huge rock up a hill each day, only to have it roll right back down just as he reached the top. Interestingly, this tedious life sentence was punishment for attempting to evade or deny death, which, as discussed in Part 1, is what we are unconsciously attempting to do when we procrastinate.

We all share a similar existential fate, in that we are each required to routinely roll our metaphorical rock—whatever that may be—uphill every day, only to have to do it all over again tomorrow. This is the inescapably repetitive nature of human existence. It is an arduous, difficult, tedious, laborious, lifelong endeavor. This monotonous, never-ending, routine, repetitive aspect of existence is something we desperately try to avoid via procrastination. We refuse to embrace the difficult, dirty, ordinary drudgery in life, distracting ourselves instead with more amusing activities. But it should be recalled that for existential philosopher Albert Camus (1955), Sisyphus eventually found meaning, satisfaction, and even contentment in accepting his mundane fate. As must we all. As philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche (1908) put it: amor fati. Love your fate. Embrace it. See it as essential, and even beautiful. Do not dismiss, dodge, or avoid it, no matter how seemingly boring, banal, or pedestrian.

The Heroic Battle Against Chronic Procrastination

A similar mythological metaphor for procrastination can be found in one of the 12 Labors of the Greek hero Hercules. Hercules was assigned the seemingly impossible task of cleaning the Augean stables, where the dung of hundreds of huge oxen had accumulated for years, in just one day. The massive stables had not been tended to for decades. Procrastination, when unchecked, creates one's own personal Augean stable.

Hercules, hesitant at first to take on this demeaning, disgusting, nasty task, but eventually employing both brain and brawn, diverts the water of two powerful rivers to get the dirty job done. (See my prior post.) Metaphorically, this represents a masterful redirection of psychic energy, libido, or the daimonic (see Diamond, 1996) and a creative utilization of available environmental resources, consciously channeling all of one's energy into the current task at hand.

This mythic story of Hercules and the Augean stables can be considered a cautionary tale for what happens when we procrastinate chronically, indefinitely, or for too long. Dung, like a neurosis, complex, or symptom, doesn't just disappear by ignoring or wishing it to. On the contrary, it intensifies over time. Toxifies. Festers. Stinks. Attracts flies and promotes disease. And becomes more, not less, difficult, noxious, and messy to deal with the longer we avoid it. This is sometimes the case with psychotherapy patients who have procrastinated for years or decades before finally seeking professional assistance for their symptoms or problems.

The Power of Presence, Will, and Mindfulness in Conquering Procrastination

People who tend to procrastinate (which includes all of us) frequently continue to do so because they feel overwhelmed or intimidated by the task facing them. Or, because they find it too tedious, undignified, or repulsive. In order to overcome procrastination, it is vital that the person consciously choose to confront rather than avoid the challenge, and accept the often tedious, ordinary, and dirty toil it demands. Simply placing one foot in front of the other rather than focusing on the enormity or monotony of the task can be one helpful trick.

In the final analysis, procrastination is a refusal or failure to be fully present to what life demands of us right now, in this moment. It is an avoidance or evasion of presence and encounter with existence, a denial of existential reality. It is an escape from mindfulness into mindlessness. In existential therapy, we recognize that to say "yes" unequivocally in any given moment to something always implies saying "no" to something else. This is what psychotherapist Otto Rank (1936) referred to as an "act of will," an unequivocal, conscious, courageous existential choice. When we exercise our will, intentionally choosing the tedious, mundane, disagreeable, distasteful, and unpalatable over the enjoyable, pleasurable, delectable, and delightful, we heroically commit ourselves to what Rank (1936) called "the willing affirmation of the must."

Some suffering, tedium, monotony, and banality is intrinsic to life, unavoidable, and must ultimately be accepted. Like Hercules, we can heroically confront, choose, or will the inevitable rather than futilely trying to escape from it. We bite the proverbial bullet. We courageously engage it willfully, passionately, creatively, and mindfully, resolutely saying "yes" to the tedious task in this present moment, and "no" to any and all other tempting distractions until the mundane task is completed to the best of our ability—at least for today, since tomorrow, as with Sisyphus, it all begins again.

But, for right now, we have temporarily conquered our procrastination, which can feel really good, empowering, and truly satisfying. Much like Sisyphus relaxing at the top of the hill after laboring all day, we have earned a brief, well-deserved reprieve, perhaps a little reward, and some much-needed rest. But, at the same time, we accept that, like Sisyphus, we must continue to roll the exact same rock uphill against gravity once more tomorrow morning. And the next. Ad infinitum, for the rest of our lives. Paradoxically, in so doing, we too can attain the contentment, happiness, or satisfaction of Sisyphus.

item.title: Using Honesty to Build a Steady Self
item.description:
Relationships

Using Honesty to Build a Steady Self

How to harness the power of truth.

Posted August 22, 2026

Key points
  • Harnessing strong self-honesty benefits us and our work with clients.
  • Reflecting on our level of honesty without criticism or judgment helps us build a steady self.
  • You can practice honesty, starting slowly as you build a stronger relationship with it.

Honesty is the bedrock of our emotional development, the primary tool for developing a strong sense of self. Our level of self-honesty dictates how much we’ll be able to see, face, work with, and change as we reach for developing a clearer sense of self. If we can’t look at our strengths and weaknesses honestly, we have little hope of truly transforming our relationship to ourselves and to our life. As therapists, our personal degree of honesty greatly impacts the depth of our work with clients.

Source: Mart Production/Pexels

Being honest with ourselves isn’t just a matter of telling the truth—it’s the most powerful and direct way to build the inner ground we stand on, the steady sense of self we long for. Being honest with ourselves means owning, facing, and grappling with our thoughts, feelings, perceptions, and choices. It entails meeting ourselves in every moment, including moments that are disappointing or frightening or confusing or challenging. The more honest we are, the more of ourselves we gain.

Here are some questions to consider:

  • Do you track your level of honesty in an ongoing way?
  • Are you aware of moments where you lean away from honesty—the situations where you hedge, omit, or outright lie?
  • Can you name the issues, people, or situations that you're not fully honest with or about, and times when you're not honest with yourself?

While we might believe absolute honesty is the best practice, we all have areas where we hold back from being completely truthful. There’s so much to learn from watching the ever-shifting edge we have between honesty and dishonesty. Being consistently aware of when we lean toward honesty and when we lean away from it tells us a lot about who we are—it’s a perfect lens.

  • Mindy always told herself the guy she was currently dating was “great,” even though she often saw early warning signs indicating the relationship wasn’t such a good choice.
  • Bruce hid expenses from his wife because she would “blow a gasket” if she knew how much he was spending on gaming; he convinced himself it was best to avoid upsetting her.
  • Tom’s deeply honest with his wife and good friends, but curates his truthfulness with his mother because of their differing values.
  • Sam grew up in an emotionally chaotic family where people lied or pretended without any regard to the fallout of those choices. Sam often felt muddled and confused (sometimes even crazy) in this atmosphere. When he left home, Sam promised himself he was always going to tell the truth, hoping that one practice would help him feel more sane and grounded in life.

The roots of dishonesty

As kids, most of us learned to manage others’ reactions: We didn’t want to make mom mad; we didn’t want dad to start yelling or hitting; we didn’t want our teacher to know we hadn’t done our homework; we didn’t want to admit we forgot a friend’s request, etc. We lied about doing our chores or where we were going or who we were hanging out with. Sometimes, lying came in handy when we wanted to look good or win an argument or get our way.

Can you imagine speaking the truth in your family, maybe saying something like:

  • “I don’t like being in this family.”
  • “You don’t really love me.”
  • “Why do we pretend all these fights are normal?”
  • “How come we ignore mom’s drinking?” (or even harsher truths)

Maybe we tried being more honest and suffered the consequences in a family with a low tolerance for the truth. Many young adults struggle to claim themselves in an honest way, moving far away instead of staying on the family farm, or choosing to be an artist instead of an engineer, or stepping away from the family’s religious beliefs to embrace a different path, etc. To manage our discomfort with upsetting others, we often begin to lie to ourselves. These kinds of choices require deep self-honesty as a first step.

Self-honesty is the foundation

Self-honesty is the most fundamental aspect of honesty. Taking stock of where we avoid telling ourselves the truth is a great place to start working with the process of truthfulness. In being dishonest with ourselves, we miss out on the crucial step of knowing—and being willing to own up to—exactly who we are. We imagine we can manage others (and ourselves), and dodge our discomfort by getting slippery with the truth. We rarely grapple with the cost of that habit of dodging honesty: a less-conscious, less clear relationship to ourselves.

Carl drove by his ex’s house a lot to keep tabs on her. “It might seem like a small thing, but I pretended I was just taking a shortcut to the mall.” As he started therapy, progress meant admitting to himself that even if he still drove toward her neighborhood, he wasn’t making a great choice. “It took me a while to stop altogether, but owning what I was doing—owning it to myself, first—was a game-changer.”

We won’t get very far in developing honesty with ourselves if we’re harsh, critical, or judgmental. We don’t need to think less of ourselves when we see where we duck out on being honest. Instead, we can bring curious compassion—a clear, open gaze. We want to have the ability to watch ourselves and compassionately say, “Oh. There. That’s where I pretended.” Or “Hmmmm...I just lied to that person.” Or “I don’t want to look at that in myself, so I’ll pretend it’s not true.”

Being honest means I don’t get to have any agenda about what I’ll face in myself. I have to let go of wanting to manage what I might see about myself. In this way, honesty is a very crucial driver for personal development. We evolve and gain more steadiness anytime we move toward being more honest with ourselves and about ourselves. I often think of honesty as the way we “regain territory” in ourselves, territory we lost or ceded in our lives; we reclaim lost aspects of self, integrity, and the kind of grounded clarity we all long for. A strong relationship to honesty gives us all of that.

Here are some typical ways we are less than honest, and things we hold back on with ourselves or others:

  • Drinking (eating, spending, being online, reading, sleeping, etc.) too much or too little, pretending we aren’t doing it
  • Pretending it’s fine, even though we don’t like that person/situation/activity
  • Smiling and nodding, when we actually wish the other person would stop talking
  • Acting like we’re clear, but feeling so unsure or clueless in ____ (a certain) situation
  • Acting like we’re OK, but feeling scared (or overwhelmed, lost, insecure, angry, lonely, fragile, etc.)
  • Pretending we’re better at our relationship than we actually are
  • Acting more sure of ourselves as a friend (parent, spouse, partner, coworker) than we feel
  • Holding back when someone asks about our feelings, mood, insights, faults

As a place to start, give yourself an assignment: Just observe your level of honesty for a week or so. Simply notice where you hedge. Don’t try to make any changes. This is a time for gathering information, seeing the baseline. No judgment, just curiosity...and coming to know yourself.

After a few days or a week of observing, pick one place (one situation, one topic, one friend, etc.) where you’d like to be more honest. Work on that. Get it solid. Then pick the next area where you’d want to step up into honesty.
